source.title: SELC: Self-Ensemble Label Correction Improves Learning with Noisy Labels

record.tranche_reason: The study measures training and test accuracy while varying label-noise levels, which bears on noisy-label fitting and generalization. It does not use fully random labels or test the other listed conditions.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports cross-entropy training and test accuracy at different label-noise ratios. Other tables report test accuracy for noisy-label methods, but do not report the random-label fitting or optimization-time outcomes in the claim. Results cited from prior work are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own SGD cross-entropy experiments measuring training fit and test accuracy under label corruption, and directly examines clean-label learning before noisy-label memorization. These bear on V4 and V6 using the original type of experiment.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but omits a central observation: predictions are relatively reliable early, before increasing memorization of wrong labels. The authors conclude that SELC uses historical predictions to correct noisy targets, prevent overfitting and improve generalization across several noise settings.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies label-noise levels and compares cross-entropy training with SELC; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.peer_reviewed: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
record.problems: The relevant accuracy results in Figure 1 are supplied only as plots, with no text-stated values or exact noise ratios. The study does not test fully random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant numerical rows beyond the figure-only training and test accuracy trends in Figure 1. The noisy-label comparison tables report test accuracy but do not give training-fit outcomes for the claim.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error and chance test performance under unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs.
The complete zero-to-total-corruption sweep, perfect training fit at every fraction, and steady test-error growth through a chance-level endpoint cannot be established from the supplied text.
Controlled comparisons of explicit regularization on fully random labels and generalization after removing regularization.
Fully random-label training and generality beyond the examined noisy-label CIFAR-10 setting.

missing.what: Clean and mislabeled sample prediction trajectories under ordinary cross-entropy: clean predictions improve, most mislabeled samples initially receive true-label predictions, and wrong-label memorization subsequently increases. Add separate rows for the sample groups and prediction categories; numerical fractions are unavailable in the supplied text.
missing.locator: Section 4.1; Figure 1(c–d), CIFAR-10 with 60% label noise

missing.what: Clean and mislabeled sample loss distributions separate early and merge again after the memorization turning point. This provides additional qualitative evidence of different learning dynamics.
missing.locator: Section 4.4; Figure 2, ResNet34 on CIFAR-10 with 60% symmetric label noise

record.verdict_notes: The reader incorrectly treats V6 as citation-only: the authors report their own relevant prediction trajectories. Missing coverage of full corruption or unavailable plot values is not evidence against a version. SELC's mitigation performance does not challenge claims about ordinary training.

versions.untested_parts: The study discusses 60% symmetric label noise, not a completely random labeling of the training set; it does not establish the full V1 condition.
Training time and convergence slowdown as corruption grows are not reported.
Shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.

Figure 1 shows accuracy across varying noise ratios, but the supplied text does not give the plotted values or enumerate the ratios. It does not establish perfect training accuracy across the full range from no corruption to all labels corrupted.
The study does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent random-label fitting, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
The study discusses learning behavior under noisy labels but does not test the real-label-first claim; Arpit et al. is cited as prior work.
